entry.summary: Every integration eventually gets the same 2 a.m. page: "The webhooks stopped working after the deploy." Nine times out of ten, nothing about the sender changed. What changed was how the receiver verified the signature — a JSON parser that re-serialized the body before hashing, a proxy that added whitespace, a framework upgrade that started decoding the payload before your middleware ran. The signature still looks almost right. It just never matches again. I build EDI and API integrations for a living, and webhook signing is where modern API practice collides with thirty years of B2B plumbing. EDI learned this lesson with AS2 message integrity checks and signed MDNs decades ago. The API world is learning it now, one broken Stripe, Shopify, or partner callback at a time. entry.title: Ceremony proportional to irreversibility: Type 1 vs Type 2 engineering decisions
entry.summary: By Decision Desk Every engineering team eventually has the same argument. One group says "we need more design review, we keep shipping things we regret." Another says "we need less process, it takes three weeks to change a config value." Both are usually right, about different decisions. The fix isn't more process or less. It's matching the process to how hard the decision is to undo. That idea has a well-known framing, and it's worth being precise about how to apply it to engineering work. Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter described two types of decisions. Type 1 decisions are "one-way doors": consequential and nearly irreversible, so they deserve slow, careful deliberation. entry.summary: Nobody reads your VEX document twice. A customer reads the first one you publish, and after that they read the difference between the new one and the copy they already hold: which advisories you have newly admitted, which conclusions you changed, which ones you have closed. entry.title: Agent user interfaces should be based on DOM, not chat
entry.summary:
Essentially all interfaces to agents are copies of each other: display some kind of history of chat/text messages. The issue with this is that it's based on "history", even though by default users don't need to scroll up and down the history, but instead want to receive the information and move on. The "chat" concept has been expanded by adding images and other rich media, even small "Apps" to the chat history. The natural evolution of this interface is leaving out the history and simply letting the agent control what information should be visualized for the user, and in what form. We can easily use DOM for this simply because agents are really good at using that interface. The agent can invent ad-hoc components required for the visualization. The exact technical solution, however, is not that important. I made a prototype for such an interface and it looks like this:
The user can talk with the agent using voice chat and natural language, and at any given time the agent can choose to show whatever is requested by the user. After the user has seen the information, the screen can be "cleared". If we try to look even more to the future, computing will likely evolve into a "one app" concept, where you only have one interface and one app to talk with the agent, and the agent will do whatever is the task. This will of course require us to think through use cases from the "first principles" instead of trying to force existing apps into this agentic UI.

entry.title: Stop picking an authorization religion
entry.summary: RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC each answer a different access question. Forcing one model to do every job is how you get role explosion and unexplainable entitlements. A practical stack: RBAC for org responsibility (tenant admin, billing manager) ABAC for runtime context (environment, sensitivity, threshold) ReBAC for ownership, sharing, and hierarchy Keep one enforcement call — can(principal, action, resource, context) — and let the policy plane mix models. Access reviews get easier when each entitlement maps to a clear reason. I work at Permit.io — we wrote a decision tree for picking the stack before the next role explosion: https://www.permit.io/blog/fga-models-decision-tree?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fga-models-decision-tree&utm_content=authbyexample-article
